- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. 19:  source: umami
21:  - "DO NOT BUILD FROM SOURCE. Umami publishes a prebuilt image and the Postgres build has its own tag: docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami:postgresql-latest. There is a ghcr.io/umami-software/umami mirror; the docs name the docker.umami.is one, so prefer it (docker.umami.is is a proxy in front of ghcr.io — a 401 on the registry API sends you to realm https://ghcr.io/token, and an anonymous pull token from there works)."
22:  - "⛔ YOU CANNOT PIN THIS BY VERSION TAG — PIN THE DIGEST, AND IT IS PROVEN TO WORK. postgresql-latest is a rolling build whose digest matches NO published version tag, so 'pin the version tag you ran' is not achievable: there isn't one. Measured TWICE, and it moved between the two: 2026-08-16 it was sha256:87312d334d009ee67ee0d2fba8fed01435547cc468e452243aef5133a9984d48 (built 2026-08-12); 2026-08-23 it was sha256:fa32d116cf20cad52cbc3fad9a63b46e7fa02299d8f967168eb453d49c476b4a (built 2026-08-20). That is a new build inside 7 days, so treat the tag as moving weekly and NEVER assume a recorded digest is still current. The newest TAGGED builds remain far older (postgresql-v2.20.2 2025-12-12, postgresql-3.0.0 2025-11-07). Re-resolve before each deploy with a HEAD on /v2/umami-software/umami/manifests/postgresql-latest and read docker-content-digest — keep the Accept header IDENTICAL between calls, because a different Accept returns a different manifest and therefore a different digest, which looks like a version change when nothing moved. CONFIRMED 2026-08-23: docker.umami.is serves manifests BY DIGEST (HEAD on the sha returns 200), an image: repo@sha256:... reference deploys cleanly, and the build log prints 'Image docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami@sha256:fa32d116... Pulled' — so the digest pin is a working reference, not just a recorded fact."
23:  - "⛔ THE LOGIN IS PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED. A fresh Umami seeds one account, username admin, and the first-login value for it is written in Umami's own public install docs. The URL is reachable from the moment the container is healthy, so between boot and the first password change ANYONE who knows the product can sign in. This is worse than an unclaimed first-run wizard: there is no window where the instance is unowned and inert. Change it the moment the deploy reports ready, before doing anything else, and hand the new value to the user in the session. CONFIRMED 2026-08-16: the seeded login signed in on the live instance on the first try, minutes after the deploy went ready."
24:  - "⛔ THE PASSWORD-CHANGE ROUTE MOVED. On current -latest builds the rotation endpoint is POST /api/me/password {currentPassword,newPassword}; the older POST /api/users/<id>/password returns 404 — and it is a Next.js HTML not-found page, NOT a JSON error, so it does not read like a routing problem at a [infra]. Hit that half-state 2026-08-16 with the instance already live on the documented default login: the sign-in step succeeded and only the rotate step failed. Try /api/me/password FIRST and fall back to the id-based path. CONFIRMED AGAIN 2026-08-23 on the 2026-08-20 build: /api/me/password answered 200 on the first attempt, so the route has been stable across two rolling builds a week apart — but keep the fallback, because the only reason it is known to move is that it already did. Cheap way to find the live route on any build: GET the candidates with the bearer token — the one that exists answers 405 (wrong method), a missing one answers 404. The login response also carries the admin user id, which is what the fallback path needs."
25:  - "⛔ SET APP_SECRET EXPLICITLY. It signs the session cookies. Left unset, Umami derives one from the database connection string, so the day anything about that string changes (a rotated database password, a rebuilt managed DB, a move between environments) every existing session is invalidated and every logged-in user is silently signed out. Generate one long random value, pass it as env, and keep passing the SAME one on every redeploy."
26:  - "DATABASE: Umami reads DATABASE_URL natively, and deploy_compose with database:'managed' APPENDS DATABASE_URL to the project .env already. This is the easy one: unlike n8n there is no remapping to do. Your compose still has to reference it explicitly (DATABASE_URL: \"${DATABASE_URL}\"), because deploy_compose writes the .env and never edits your compose file. Umami creates its own tables inside whatever database it is given. Managed-DB defaults ARE database `app` and user `appuser`, which is fine — do not misread the reports: get_deployment calls the datastore `umami` and list_databases shows `name: umami`, but that is the managed-DB RESOURCE name (taken from the deployment name, VM `db-umami`); `db_name` inside it is still `app`. Deploy #419: resource `umami`, db_name `app`, db_user `appuser`."
27:  - "⛔ DO NOT ADD CLICKHOUSE. The redu MCP has a standing rule that analytics apps which store every event (Plausible, PostHog, Matomo, SigNoz) need a SECOND datastore and tells you to pass needs_clickhouse:true. Umami on the postgresql image does NOT: it stores events in the same Postgres. There is a separate ClickHouse build of Umami, and this is not it. Following the general rule here provisions a whole managed ClickHouse the app never connects to, and quietly doubles the bill."
28:  - "PORT 3000. The container listens there and the healthcheck Umami ships hits http://localhost:3000/api/heartbeat, which is also the cheapest thing to curl from the VM to prove the app is really up rather than merely running."
29:  - "NO migrate_command NEEDED. Umami runs its own Prisma migrations at container start. On a fresh managed Postgres the first boot takes noticeably longer than later ones while it creates the schema; that is not a hang."
30:  - "TRACKING SCRIPT: the snippet Umami hands you points at /script.js on the instance's own hostname, so it works on the *.redu.cloud URL with no extra wiring. If the user later moves it to their own domain, the snippet they already pasted into their site keeps pointing at the old host."
33:  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source, so there is no repo to point deploy_compose at. Write a one-service docker-compose.yml locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Passing the Umami GitHub URL would make redu try to build the app instead of pulling the published image."
34:  - "VERIFY APP_SECRET WITHOUT SSH — get_env_keys DOES IT. The 2026-08-16 run had to record 'APP_SECRET present inside the container' as UNVERIFIED because the confirming SSH command was blocked. There is no need for a shell: get_env_keys returns the KEY NAMES in /opt/app-src/.env (values never leave the VM) and that is the whole question — did the variable get wired, or is the app reading a name nobody set. Confirmed 2026-08-23: APP_SECRET present alongside DATABASE_URL/PG*, file mode 600 root:root. get_containers/get_container_logs/get_resource_usage answer the rest of the 'deployed but broken' questions the same way."
37:  - "THE DEPLOY VM RUNS DOCKER, NOT PODMAN, despite deploy_compose's own description saying podman-compose. The compose project is named app-src, so the container is app-src-umami-1 and volumes are app-src_<name>; use `sudo docker ...` if you do SSH in."
38:  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. redu.md is committed and read by the next person. The admin password you set and the APP_SECRET you generate are the user's, not yours to publish. Hand both over in the session and tell them to store them. The deploy log records THAT the account was secured, never what it was secured with."
